column1: # Shared aontu unit tests: the number model. Columns (tab-separated): name<TAB>mode<TAB>src<TAB>expect
# mode: canon = unify(src).canon == expect ; gen = generate(src) deep-equals JSON(expect) ; err = generate(src) errors, message contains expect
# See docs/design/number-model.md for the rules these rows pin.
# R1: a numeric literal has integer kind iff its source has no '.', its
# value is integral, and it lies within the int64 range. Otherwise it is
# number kind. (aontu has no negative literals -- '-' is an operator --
# so the int64 minimum is not expressible as an integer-kind literal.)
# A literal above 2^53 is stored in IEEE-754 double precision and is
# therefore not exact; both implementations agree on the rounded value.
# R2: negative zero never survives into the AST, generated output, or canon.
# R3: concrete scalars are identical only when kind and value both match,
# so an integer and a float disjunct member are distinct alternatives.
# R4: canon round-trips kind -- a number-kind value always renders with a
# fraction or an exponent, so parse(canon(v)) preserves the kind of v.
# R5: kind contagion -- no operator or function introduces a narrower kind
# than its operands. integer+integer is integer; any number operand makes
# the result a number; upper()/lower() preserve the argument's kind.
# R6: super(x) is the lattice-superior of its argument -- the kind of a
# concrete scalar. (1 is an integer literal, so super(1) is integer.)
# NaN and Infinity are NOT numeric literals in aontu: they carry no
# special lexing, so they are bare text and unify as strings. (There
# is no way to write a non-finite number: an overflowing literal is a
# Leading zeros are decimal, never octal (08 and 09 are 8 and 9, not
# errors). A LEADING dot is not a numeric literal at all -- a bare
# dotted word is a relative path reference, so .5 is an unresolvable
# A numeric map KEY is not a number: the key keeps its source text
# verbatim, so it is never normalised through the number model.
# There are no negative literals: `-` is a prefix operator. It binds
# TIGHTER than `+`, `&` and `|` (and looser than `.`), so `-1 & -1` is
# `(-1) & (-1)`, not `-(1 & -1)`. Negation never narrows the kind.
# Base prefixes (hex/octal/binary) are LOWER CASE ONLY: an upper-case
# prefix is not a number at all, it is text. That follows the canonical
# TypeScript lexer, whose number matcher spells the prefixes in lower
# case; the Go engine declines the same sources (numberExcluded in
# go/lang.go) so the two agree. Note it is the prefix LETTER only -- an
# upper-case exponent marker is accepted by both (exp-upper-canon).
# A based literal has no '.', so R1(b)+(c) alone decide its kind:
# 0x7fffffffffffffff rounds up to 2^63 and so is number kind, which is
# Digit separators are legal only as a SINGLE separator BETWEEN
# digits. A run that breaks the rule is not a number at all: the whole
# run falls through to text, so a typo surfaces as a string rather
# than silently becoming a different number (1__0 is "1__0", not 10).
# The base-prefixed edge cases are pinned at both magnitudes because
# a literal beyond int64 takes a separate lexer path in the Go port.
# Exponent forms. The exponent marker may be upper or lower case and
# its sign is optional; an exponent alone never makes a literal number
# kind (R1 looks for a '.', not an 'e'), so 1e3 and even the
# UNDERFLOWING 1e-400 -- which is exactly 0 -- are integer kind and
# canon them without a ".0". An OVERFLOWING literal is a not_number
# A numeric builtin called with no argument is an invalid-arg error
# value, not an internal error: reading the argument off nothing used
# to throw in TypeScript, which the unifier could only report as an
# opaque internal failure while Go reported it cleanly.
